title.en: The Great Hymn to Amen-Ra, Bull of Karnak

region.en: Thebes, Egypt (temple of Amen-Ra at Karnak)
region.zh: 埃及底比斯（卡納克阿蒙-拉神廟）

texts.period: New Kingdom hymn, c. 1600-900 BCE (Cairo papyrus; Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. XII, the Hymn to Amen-Ra

summary.en: The state hymn of the New Kingdom temple: Amen-Ra is hailed as the Bull of Karnak, the hidden creator who suspends the sky and hammers out the earth, maker of men and gods, one in form yet of many names, whose hidden name 'Amen' conceals him even from his own children the gods.
summary.zh: 新王國神廟國頌：阿蒙-拉被尊為卡納克之牛、懸天錘地之隱名造物主，造人亦造神，形一而名多——其隱名『阿蒙』連諸神子女亦不得窺知。

sensitivity.note: Ancient temple hymn quoted for comparative scholarship; no living community restrictions. Budge's 1910 wording is the cited public-domain source, presented without religious truth claims.

passages.text: Homage to thee, Amen-Ra, Lord of the throne of Egypt. Master of the Apts (Karnak). Kamutef at the head of his fields. The long-strider, Master of the Land of the South. Lord of the Matchau (Nubians), Governor of Punt, King of heaven, first-born son of earth, Lord of things that are, stablisher of things (i.e. the universe), stablisher of all things. One in his actions, as with the gods, Beneficent Bull of the Company of the Gods (or of the Nine Gods), Chief of all the gods, Lord of Truth, father of the gods, maker of men, creator of all animals, Lord of things that are, creator of the staff of life, Maker of the herbage that sustaineth the life of cattle.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), ch. XII, Hymn to Amen-Ra, sections II-III.

passages.text: The gods fall down awestruck at his feet, when they recognise His Majesty their Lord. Lord of terror, great one of victory, Great one of Souls, mighty one of crowns. He maketh offerings abundant, [and] createth food. Praise be unto thee, creator of the gods. Suspender of the sky, who hammered out the earth. — Homage to thee, Ra, Lord of Truth. Hidden is the shrine of the Lord of the gods. Khepera in his boat giveth the order, and the gods come into being. [He is] Tem, maker of the Rekhit beings, however many be their forms he maketh them to live, distinguishing one kind from another.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), sections VI and X.

passages.text: He heareth the cry of him that is oppressed. He is gracious of heart to him that appealeth to him. He delivereth the timid man from the man of violence. He regardeth the poor man and considereth [his] misery. He is the lord Sa (i.e. Taste); abundance is his utterance. The Nile cometh at his will. He is the lord of graciousness, who is greatly beloved. He cometh and sustaineth mankind. He setteth in motion everything that is made. He worketh in the Celestial Water, making to be the pleasantness of the light.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), sections XI-XII.

passages.text: He is Ra who is worshipped in the Apts. He is the one of many crowns in the House of the Benben Stone. He is the god Ani, the lord of the ninth-day festival. He maketh himself to be seen in the horizon, Chief of the beings of the Other World. His name is hidden from the gods who are his children, in his name of 'Amen.' — [He is] the Form One, the creator of everything that is. The One only, the creator of things that shall be. Men and women proceeded from his two eyes. His utterance became the gods. He maketh to live the fish in the river, and the geese and the feathered fowl of the sky. He giveth air to the creature that is in the egg.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), sections XIII and XV.

title.en: The Hymn to Amen: All the Gods Are Three

region.zh: 埃及底比斯（萊頓紙草，底比斯神學）

texts.period: New Kingdom hymn, c. 1550-1200 BCE (Leyden papyrus; Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. XII, the Leyden papyrus extract on the power and glory of Amen

summary.en: A Theban hymn of divine omnipotence: Amen heals without medicine, rescues the doomed, stills the crocodile when his name is spoken, and stands behind the triune face of godhead — his face is Ra, his body Ptah — while the Nile rises from the hollow beneath his sandals and the luck and destiny of every man are in his hand.
summary.zh: 底比斯頌歌詠神之全能：阿蒙不假藥物而醫眼，救溺水者於冥府，其名一呼鱷魚失力；眾神合三為一——拉為其面，卜塔為其身；尼羅自其履下之穴湧出，萬民命運皆在其手。

sensitivity.note: Ancient temple hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: He driveth away evils and scattereth diseases. He is the physician who healeth the eye without [the use of] medicaments. He openeth the eyes, he driveth away inflammation. He delivereth whom he pleaseth, even from the Tuat (the Other World). He saveth a man from what is ordained for him at the dictates of his heart. To him belong both eyes and ears, [he is] on every path of him whom he loveth. He heareth the petitions of him that appealeth to him. He cometh from afar to him that calleth [before] a moment hath passed.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), ch. XII, the Leyden papyrus extract.

passages.text: He maketh high (i.e. long) the life [of a man], he cutteth it short. To him whom he loveth he giveth more than hath been fated for him. [When] Amen casteth a spell on the water, and his name is on the waters, if this name of his be uttered the crocodile hath no power. The winds are driven back, the hurricane is repulsed. At the remembrance of him the wrath of the angry man dieth down. He speaketh the gentle word at the moment of strife. He is a pleasant breeze to him that appealeth to him. He delivereth the helpless one. He is more helpful than millions to the man who hath set him in his heart. One warrior [who fighteth] under his name is better than hundreds of thousands.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Leyden papyrus extract.

passages.text: All the gods are three, Amen, Ra and Ptah, and there are none like unto them. He whose name is hidden is Amen. Ra belongeth to him as his face, and his body is Ptah. Their cities are established upon the earth for ever, [namely,] Thebes, Anu (Heliopolis), and Hetkaptah (Memphis). When a message is sent from heaven it is heard in Anu, and is repeated in Memphis to the Beautiful Face (i.e. Ptah). It is done into writing, in the letters of Thoth (i.e. hieroglyphs), and despatched to the City of Amen (i.e. Thebes), with their things.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Leyden papyrus extract.

passages.text: His heart is Understanding, his lips are Taste, his Ka is all the things that are in his mouth. He entereth, the two caverns are beneath his feet. The Nile appeareth from the hollow beneath his sandals. His soul is Shu, his heart is Tefnut. He is Heru-Khuti in the upper heaven. His right eye is day. His left eye is night. He is the leader of faces on every path. His body is Nu. The dweller in it is the Nile, producing everything that is, nourishing all that is. He breatheth breath into all nostrils. The Luck and the Destiny of every man are with him. His wife is the earth, he uniteth with her, his seed is the tree of life, his emanations are the grain.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Leyden papyrus extract.

title.en: Hymn to the Sun-god: The Judge of Words and Deeds

region.en: Cairo limestone ostracon provenance, New Kingdom Egypt
region.zh: 新王國埃及（開羅石灰岩陶片出土語境）

texts.period: New Kingdom hymn written on limestone slices, c. 1300-1100 BCE (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. XII, 'Hymns to the Sun-god'

summary.en: On a schoolboy's limestone slice a New Kingdom hymn praises the child of fire who sails the sky: he destroys the serpent-fiend Neka with the help of the Children of Horus, becomes Tem at evening to comfort the dead, and sits as Judge of words and deeds — to whom the hymnist prays that a wrongful usurper of his office be judged rightly.
summary.zh: 書童陶片上新王國頌詩讚火之子——日行天穹之童神：賀魯斯諸子合力誅蛇魔內卡；暮為阿圖姆而撫亡者；居於言行之審判座——頌者祈其審理奪其官職之不義者。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Well dost thou watch, O Horus, who sailest over the sky, thou child who proceedest from the divine father, thou child of fire, who shinest like crystal, who destroyest the darkness and the night. Thou child who growest rapidly, with gracious form, who restest in thine eye. Thou wakest up men who are asleep on their beds, and the reptiles in their nests. Thy boat saileth on the fiery Lake Neserser, and thou traversest the upper sky by means of the winds thereof.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), ch. XII, Hymns to the Sun-god.

passages.text: The two daughters of the Nile-god crush for thee the fiend Neka, Nubti (i.e. Set) pierceth him with his arrows. Keb seizeth (?) him by the joint of his back, Serqet grippeth him at his throat. The flame of this serpent that is over the door of thy house burneth him up. The Great Company of the Gods are wroth with him, and they rejoice because he is cut to pieces. The Children of Horus grasp their knives, and inflict very many gashes in him. Hail! Thine enemy hath fallen, and Truth standeth firm before thee.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Hymns to the Sun-god.

passages.text: When thou again transformest thyself into Tem, thou givest thy hand to the Lords of Akert (i.e. the dead), those who lie in death give thanks for thy beauties when thy light falleth upon them. They declare unto thee what is their hearts' wish, which is that they may see thee again. When thou hast passed them by, the darkness covereth them, each one in his coffin. Thou art the lord of those who cry out (?) to thee, the god who is beneficent for ever.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Hymns to the Sun-god.

passages.text: Thou art the Judge of words and deeds, the Chief of chief judges, who stablisheth truth, and doest away sin. May he who attacketh me be judged rightly, behold, he is stronger than I am; he hath seized upon my office, and hath carried it off with falsehood. May it be restored to me.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Hymns to the Sun-god, closing petition.

title.en: The Hymn to Shu: He Who Stretches Out the Heavens

region.en: British Museum Magical Papyrus (Harris No. 501), Egypt
region.zh: 埃及（大英博物館魔法紙草哈里斯501號）

texts.period: Late New Kingdom / Third Intermediate hymn, c. 1100-900 BCE (Budge translation 1910)

source.work: The Literature of the Ancient Egyptians, trans. E. A. W. Budge (1910), ch. XII, the Hymn to Shu

summary.en: A hymn to the air-god Shu, flesh and bone of Ra and his firstborn son: he drives his spear into the serpent-fiend Nekau daily, Tefnut rides his head hurling fire at enemies, and he stretches out the heavens with his own hands — the self-created son who had no mother, twice great above the gods.
summary.zh: 頌大氣之神舒——拉之血肉長子：日日持矛刺蛇魔內考；泰芙努特踞其首，擲火焚敵；彼以雙手撐天——無母而自生之子，凌駕諸神兩倍之尊。

sensitivity.note: Ancient hymn from a magical papyrus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Homage to thee, O flesh and bone of Ra, thou first-born son who didst proceed from his members, who wast chosen to be the chief of those who were brought forth, thou mighty one, thou divine form, who art endowed with strength as the lord of transformations. Thou overthrowest the Seba fiends each day. The divine boat hath the wind [behind it], thy heart is glad. Those who are in the Antti Boat utter loud cries of joy when they see Shu, the son of Ra, triumphant, [and] driving his spear into the serpent fiend Nekau.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), ch. XII, Hymn to Shu.

passages.text: Ra setteth out to sail over the heavens at dawn daily. The goddess Tefnut is seated on thy head, she hurleth her flames of fire against thy enemies, and maketh them to be destroyed utterly. Thou art equipped by Ra, thou art mighty through his words of power, thou art the heir of thy father upon his throne, and thy Doubles rest in the Doubles of Ra, even as the taste of what hath been in the mouth remaineth therein.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Hymn to Shu.

passages.text: Homage to thee, O son of Ra, who wast begotten by Temu himself. Thou didst create thyself, and thou hadst no mother. Thou art Truth, the lord of Truth, thou art the Power, the ruling power of the gods. Thou dost conduct the Eye of thy father Ra. They give gifts unto thee into thine own hands. Thou makest to be at peace the Great Goddess, when storms are passing over her. Thou dost stretch out the heavens on high, and dost establish them with thine own hands.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Hymn to Shu.

passages.text: Every god boweth in homage before thee, the King of the South, the King of the North, Shu, the son of Ra, life, strength and health be to thee! Thou, O great god Pautti, art furnished with the brilliance of the Eye [of Ra] in Heliopolis, to overthrow the Seba fiends on behalf of thy father. Thou makest the divine Boat to sail onwards in peace. The mariners who are therein exult, and all the gods shout for joy when they hear thy divine name. Greater, yea greater (i.e. twice great) art thou than the gods in thy name of Shu, son of Ra.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1910), Hymn to Shu, closing.

title.en: The Great Hymn to the Aten: One God Over All Lands
title.zh: 阿頓大頌：萬國唯一之神

region.en: Akhet-Aten (Amarna), Egypt (tomb of Ay, where the hymn is inscribed)
region.zh: 埃及阿赫頓-阿頓（阿馬爾納，阿伊墓刻壁處）

texts.period: Composed under Akhenaten, c. 1350-1334 BCE (tomb of Ay at Amarna; Budge translation 1923)

source.archive: Wikisource (from Budge, Tutankhamen: Amenism, Atenism and Egyptian Monotheism, 1923)
source.work: A Hymn of praise of Her-aakhuti (the Great Hymn to Aten), composed by Akhenaten, trans. E. A. Wallis Budge (1923)

summary.en: The most radical text of pharaonic religion: the sun's disk alone creates and sustains everything — people of every tongue and skin, beasts, fish, the chick in the egg — setting a Nile for foreign lands and a Nile in the underworld for Egypt; only Akhenaten, his son, knows him, and all other gods have been effaced from the world.
summary.zh: 法老宗教中最激進之文本：太陽之盤獨自創造並養活萬有——異語異膚之眾民、走獸游魚、卵中之雛——為外邦置天之尼羅，為埃及置冥府之尼羅；唯其子阿肯那頓識之，餘神盡廢於世。

sensitivity.note: Ancient royal hymn; no living community restrictions. Category 'religious' chosen deliberately: this is canonical liturgy of the Aten cult composed by the king himself, unlike the narrative myths of the tradition.

passages.text: Thy rising [is] beautiful in the horizon of heaven, O Aten, ordainer of life. Thou dost shoot up in the horizon of the East, thou fillest every land with thy beneficence. Thou art beautiful and great and sparkling, and exalted above every land. Thy arrows (i.e., rays) envelop (i.e., penetrate) everywhere all the lands which thou hast made. Thou art as Ra. Thou bringest [them] according to their number, thou subduest them for thy beloved son. Thou thyself art afar off, but thy beams are upon the earth; thou art in their faces, they [admire] thy goings.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge, Tutankhamen (1923), the Great Hymn to Aten (tomb of Ay), sections 2-3.

passages.text: Thou settest in the horizon of the west, the earth is in darkness, in the form of death. Men lie down in a booth wrapped up in cloths, one eye cannot see its fellow. If all their possessions, which are under their heads, be carried away they perceive it not. Every lion emergeth from his lair, all the creeping things bite, darkness [is] a warm retreat. The land is in silence. He who made them hath set in his horizon. The earth becometh light, thou shootest up in the horizon, shining in the Aten in the day, thou scatterest the darkness. Thou sendest out thine arrows (i.e., rays), the Two Lands make festival, [men] wake up, stand upon their feet, it is thou who raisest them up.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1923), sections 3-4.

passages.text: O how many are the things which thou hast made! They are hidden from the face, O thou One God, like whom there is no other. Thou didst create the earth by thy heart (or will), thou alone existing, men and women, cattle, beasts of every kind that are upon the earth, and that move upon feet (or legs), all the creatures that are in the sky and that fly with their wings, [and] the deserts of Syria and Kesh (Nubia), and the Land of Egypt. Thou settest every person in his place. Thou providest their daily food, every man having the portion allotted to him, [thou] dost compute the duration of his life. Their tongues are different in speech, their characteristics (or forms), and likewise their skins [in colour], giving distinguishing marks to the dwellers in foreign lands.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1923), sections 7-9.

passages.text: Thou settest a Nile in heaven, which cometh down to them. It maketh a flood on the mountains like the Great Green Sea, it maketh to be watered their fields in their villages. How beneficent are thy plans, O Lord of Eternity! A Nile in heaven art thou for the dwellers in the foreign lands (or deserts), and for all the beasts of the desert that go upon feet (or legs). Hapi (the Nile) cometh from the Tuat for the land of Egypt. Thy beams nourish every field; thou risest up [and] they live, they germinate for thee. Thou hast made millions of creations (or, evolutions) from thy one self (viz.) towns and cities, villages, fields, roads and river. Every eye (i.e., all men) beholdeth thee confronting it. Thou art the Aten of the day at its zenith.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Budge (1923), sections 9-11.

texts.language: Egyptian (New Kingdom, late Middle Egyptian, wall inscription)
texts.canonical_translation: E. A. Wallis Budge, Tutankhamen: Amenism, Atenism and Egyptian Monotheism (London, 1923), 'A Hymn to Aten' (tomb of Ay)

narrative.en:
The Great Hymn to the Aten is the centerpiece of the most ambitious religious revolution Egypt ever attempted. About year 5 of his reign, the king Amenhotep IV renamed himself Akhenaten ('Effective for the Aten'), abandoned Thebes and the temples of Amun, and built a new capital, Akhet-Aten ('Horizon of the Aten', modern Amarna), where the sun's disk alone was worshipped. The Great Hymn, composed in the king's own voice or court circle, was carved in the tombs of his nobles at Amarna — most completely in the tomb of Ay, later Tutankhamun's successor — so that its words would be forever available to the dead.

THE HYMN'S ARGUMENT. Unlike every other Egyptian hymn, which piles up epithets of one god among many, the Great Hymn describes a single creator whose power is light itself. Aten rises in the east and 'fillest every land with thy beneficence'; his rays are hands that 'subduest them for thy beloved son.' At sunset the world falls into darkness 'in the form of death': lions emerge, serpents bite, and a man's own possessions could be stolen over his head without his perceiving it. At dawn the Two Lands make festival, and every creature — cattle, birds, fish in the river, boats on the Nile — moves by the light's command.

CREATION BY LIGHT ALONE. The hymn then universalizes the creator. The Aten 'didst create the earth by thy heart, thou alone existing': men and women, cattle, birds, the creatures of Syria, Nubia, and Egypt alike. He sets every person in his place, apportions his food, and computes his lifespan. He gives each people its own tongue, form, and skin color — a striking acceptance of difference as divine ordinance rather than disorder. For the foreign lands he 'settest a Nile in heaven', a rain-flood watering their fields from the sky; for Egypt the true Nile rises 'from the Tuat', the underworld, by the god's plan. Even the unborn are his: the chick speaks in the shell, and the Aten gives it breath to crack the egg from within.

THE SOLITARY KING. The hymn's most exclusive claim comes near its close: 'Thou art in my heart. There is no other who knoweth thee except thy son Nefer-kheperu-Ra Ua-en-Ra' — Akhenaten alone understands the Aten's plans and power. The world that was 'millions of creations' from the one self is governed through one man. The hymn closes with the royal family named — the king 'great in the duration of his life' and Nefertiti 'living and young for ever and ever' — binding creation, light, and dynasty into one circuit.

HISTORY AND FAILURE. Within a generation of Akhenaten's death the temples of Amun were restored, Amarna was demolished, and the Aten hymns were chiseled out — surviving only because tomb walls hid them from the erasers. Egyptologists read the hymn both as the culmination of the old solar theology of Ra (the same creator-god by heart and tongue that the creation legends describe) and as the ancestor of a monotheistic form that would not recur in Egypt. It functions in this corpus as the tradition's most radical creation-and-theophany text, the pole at which Egyptian hymnody becomes exclusive religion.

functions: State liturgy of the Aten cult, carved in nobles' tombs for the eternal benefit of the dead
Exposition of solar monotheism: one creator known through light alone, without myth or temple image
Universalist theology of difference: every people given its own tongue, form, and skin by divine ordinance
Royal ideology: the sole god is known only through the sole king, Akhenaten and his household

variants.name: Shorter Hymn to the Aten (same Amarna corpus)
variants.text_tradition: Amarna tombs (Meryre II, Huya, Ay, Mahu), c. 1350-1334 BCE
variants.summary: A shorter, less radical hymn to the Aten survives in several Amarna tombs, hailing the rising sun in language close to traditional solar hymns; the Great Hymn's universalism and exclusive claims mark it as the genre's culmination.

variants.name: Traditional solar hymns (Ra-Khepera dawn hymn)
variants.text_tradition: Book of the Dead ch. 15, Papyrus of Ani, New Kingdom
variants.summary: The pre-revolution dawn liturgy hails Khepera rising amid a plural pantheon — Thoth, Maat, the celestial ferry — with the deceased petitioning for a seat in the solar barque; the Aten hymn strips out every god but the disk and its king.

variants.name: Restoration aftermath: Amun restored, Aten erased
variants.text_tradition: Restoration Stela of Tutankhamun (c. 1332 BCE, Cairo JE 31882)
variants.summary: Tutankhamun's Restoration Stela records temples of the gods fallen into ruin 'as if they had never been' during the Aten interlude and their refoundation under Amun — the state's official undoing of the hymn's world.

primary_sources.work: The Great Hymn to the Aten (A Hymn of Praise of Her-aakhuti)

Budge, Tutankhamen: Amenism, Atenism and Egyptian Monotheism (London, 1923), pp. 122-135. (Attribution to Akhenaten himself follows the tomb inscriptions; some scholars assign the text to Ay's circle.)
